sources.description: OKKO FX BFGRMWB: a boutique Green Russian Big Muff recreation tuned to a vintage Bubble Font unit, with added Mid Range, Rumble and Presence controls.
sources.snippet: OKKO FX BFGRMWB Demo Review | Loopy Demos
sources.bodyExcerpt: --> OKKO FX BFGRMWB Demo Review | Loopy Demos Show or hide the side bar navigation Loopy Demos Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact All demos OKKO FX BFGRMWB Oct 6, 2024 Read next Budget Guitar Pedals That Sound Expensive: Best Value Effects Under $150 The BFGRMWB stands for Big Fucking Green Russian Muff With Benefits. This handwired pedal out of Leipzig was tuned to a particular early V7D Bubble Font vintage Russian Big Muff: the unit known for its bold, powerful character. Then OKKO FX added three extra controls to make it practical in a modern rig. Plug in, stomp the switch, and it’s immediately clear why people keep coming back to the Russian Muff sound. Controls The panel splits into two columns. On the left are the two large knobs: Distortion at the top and Volume below it. On the right, four smaller knobs run from top to bottom: Tone, Mid Range, Rumble, and Presence. Distortion and Volume do what you’d expect from a Muff: Distortion covers everything from light grit up to a wall of sustain, and Volume makes up any level lost in the clipping. Tone is the classic Muff tone stack, brightest counterclockwise and darkest clockwise, with the sweet spot depending on your pickup and amp. The three extra knobs are where this pedal earns its subtitle. Mid Range adjusts how much midrange presence you get: back off for a deeper scoop, push it for more punch and cut. Rumble controls how much bass enters the circuit. Full open is the stock vintage setting, great for bass or a driven amp; rolled back it tightens up the low end for a high-headroom clean amp. Presence handles the top-end shimmer: back off for bright rigs, push it if you need definition to cut through a mix. In the demo above I’ve set up sweeps for Distortion, Tone, Mid Range, Rumble, and Presence, so you can hear each control do its work in isolation. How It Sounds Russian Muffs sit in a different part of the family tree than the NYC variants: more midrange presence, a rawer low end, and a quality that reads as more aggressive even at lower gain settings. The BFGRMWB captures that and then gives you knobs to push it further or pull it back. The Russian Default preset puts the pedal in roughly stock vintage territory. Heavy Sizzle cranks Distortion and Presence for maximum fizz and grind. Extra Scoop drops Mid Range down and shows how much of a difference that control makes. Nice Drive rolls back Distortion with Rumble wide open for a driven-amp texture that stays on the fuzz side of overdrive. The preset cheekily named “The perfect Muff doesn’t exist” dials everything in together for the sustained, thick tone that made the original Bubble Font units famous. BFGRMWB vs Big Muff PI The EHX Big Muff PI is the natural cross-shop. The Muff gives you one classic sound: thick, smooth, and scooped. Adjust the tone knob to your rig and let it rip. The BFGRMWB starts from a Russian Bubble Font reference rather than a New York one, and adds six controls where the Muff has three, so you get more bass weight, more midrange presence, and more top-end control. It’s harder to find, released only in batches. If the iconic scooped sound and simplicity are what you want, the EHX is hard to argue with. If you want that rawer, fuller Russian character tuned precisely to your amp, the BFGRMWB gives you headroom the original never had. Who It’s For It’s a natural fit for anyone who’s loved Green Russian Big Muffs but found them hard to tame: too much bass flub through a clean amp, not enough definition to cut a mix, or the mid scoop sitting wrong in a band context. The extra controls solve all three without changing the core character. It works for guitar, bass, and baritone. If you want a smooth, scooped Muff with no extra shaping to manage, the NYC Big Muff is the simpler option. If the Russian sound is what you’re after and you want it dialed in, this is the pedal. sources.bodyExcerpt: --> OKKO FX MOTÖRBASS Demo Review | Loopy Demos Show or hide the side bar navigation Loopy Demos Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact Demos Posts Manufacturers About Contact All demos OKKO FX MOTÖRBASS Oct 4, 2023 Read next What is the Best Bass Overdrive Pedal? The MOTÖRBASS by OKKO FX is one of those pedals I honestly didn’t expect to fall for. I’ve never been a Motörhead devotee, and recreating Lemmy’s bass tone isn’t exactly on my to-do list. But what OKKO has built here goes well beyond a tribute. It’s a straightforward, punchy bass distortion that plays well in a rock mix without eating your low end alive. The way the bass functions in Motörhead is almost like a second rhythm guitar: heavily distorted, loaded with mids. That’s not a tone I’d reach for in most of my mixes. But the MOTÖRBASS surprised me by adding mids and highs in just the right proportions, so the bass still sounds like bass. It cuts through the guitars without turning to mush. That combination of aggression and clarity is harder to find than you’d think. Controls Three controls, clearly named. FASTER is gain, running from almost clean up to full blast. LOUDER is volume. HARDER shapes the upper mids: turned down it stays rounded and thick, turned up it adds aggressive bite and attack. Panel order from left to right: FASTER and LOUDER sit side by side as the two large knobs, with HARDER as a smaller knob tucked below center. In the demo above I’ve set up sweeps for both FASTER and HARDER so you can hear what each one does across its full range. How It Sounds “Tamed Beast” shows the pedal at restrained gain with a moderate HARDER setting, just enough grit to give the bass presence without shredding the signal. Crank FASTER and HARDER up for “Bare Teeth” and the upper mids bite hard while the low end holds firm underneath. “Full Roar” pushes gain and volume both to ten: grinding, full, and surprisingly usable in context. “Fat Punch” brings everything to noon as a balanced reference point. What I keep coming back to is how little I need to touch the EQ after recording with this pedal. The gain structure is gnarly but controlled, and the HARDER knob handles the tonal shaping in a way that lands without extra surgery in post. It also works as a light boost to push the front end of an amp. And yes, I’ve tested it on guitar: it stacks well and sounds great, though bass is clearly where it lives. MOTÖRBASS vs Basstortion The ZVEX Basstortion is the obvious cross-shop here: three controls, designed specifically for bass, and built around retaining low end under distortion. The Basstortion leans brighter and more open-sounding, especially in its Bright mode, which gives it a more guitar-like clang. The MOTÖRBASS is thicker and more mid-forward by default, sitting deeper in the mix rather than cutting across it. The Basstortion also has a DARK mode that smooths the top end out considerably, making it the more flexible option between the two if you need a wider range of characters. The MOTÖRBASS has a more focused identity: aggressive, punchy mid-driven rock distortion. Less range, but a stronger personality in that lane. Who It’s For Rock and hard rock bass players who want a distortion that adds mid-range presence without thinning out the low end. It’s well suited to shortscale basses, flatwounds, and pick playing, which is how I run it. If your ideal bass distortion is bright and cutting rather than thick and grindy, the MOTÖRBASS probably isn’t your pedal. If you want something that gets out of the way and makes every heavy backing track sound better without a second thought, it’s hard to argue with. sources.h1: Beam Splitter V2
sources.description: Beam Splitter takes one signal and makes three copies of it, taking three different overdrive voices and sending two of them through individual delay lines. It is specifically our way of creating a huge sound out of a regular one. Output can be kept in parallel mono, spread out in stereo, or further split into three outputs (what we call “trereo”). While the goal is singular bigness, you can create classic drives, flangers, lofi vibratos, trailing slapback echoes, and more using the full control set. Beam Splitter V2 has: Buffered trails or true bypass switching Presets Expression control over every knob MIDI control over everything in the pedal Mono or stereo input (stereo will be collapsed to mono when the pedal is on), and mono, stereo, or trereo output Controls include: Gain , Volume , and Tone to shape the amount of distortion, overall volume, and brightness of each drive section Time and Feedback controls for each delay to set the timing (up to 211mS) and the amount of resonance or decay Deviate to randomly vary the delay time, giving a more natural feel and chorus effect Spread to set the amount of stereo spread Delay Select to choose which drives are delayed For more information, see the Beam Splitter V2 manual available here . Requires 9V DC center negative 2.1mm jack power supply capable of 350mA (not included). The art of Beam Splitter is by Dustin Charles.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Beam Splitter V2 by Old Blood Noise Endeavors | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Old Blood Noise Endeavors Beam Splitter V2 LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS OVERDRIVE DISTORTION DELAY CHORUS FLANGER Description Splitting an incoming instrument signal into three distinct parallel overdrive voices, two lines feed into independent delay lines to emulate triple-tracked textures. The first channel features hard-clipping distortion, the second employs a brighter mix of soft and hard clipping, and the revoiced third section provides dynamic transistor drive. Flexible routing allows users to assign delays to any two channels while shaping resonance, delay time up to 211 ms, and stereo or trereo output width. Modulation unfolds through a dedicated deviate parameter that injects randomized delay time fluctuations reminiscent of organic multi-tracking inaccuracies. Modern hardware enhancements deliver three footswitches, full MIDI integration across all parameters, onboard presets, and versatile expression assignments for every knob. Combining digital control with analog drive paths, the pedal achieves everything from classic dirt and slapback repeats to resonant flanging and wide chorusing. sources.description: Pardner is a whacky fuzz with unique synthy textures that resonate and warble and pair with an overdriven effects loop (“Lasso”) to add further textures to an already otherworldly dirt device. Rip a solo or some massive chords or heck, run your drums through it - we’re not here to tell you how to Pardner. Controls include: Filter and Intensity and Synthy-Fuzzy toggle to shape the core voice of the fuzz Treble , Bass , and Fuzz Volume to sculpt the fuzz output Lasso Gain and Lasso Volume to set the overdrive amount and volume of the Lasso effects loop Lasso Out (Send) and Lasso In (Return) jacks to route other effects into Pardner Lasso First-Para-Fuzz First toggle to set the order of effects Individual soft-touch bypass footswitches for each side, with true relay bypass when both sides are off For more information, see the Pardner manual available here. Requires 9V DC center negative 2.1mm jack power supply capable of 80mA (not included). Dimensions: 4.25” (width) x 5” (height) x 2” (depth). The art of Pardner is by Garrett Young. https://doctopmaru.tumblr.com/

The gain structure is produced using single-ended JFET circuitry running in Class A, just like a valve amp. The input buffer, output buffer and Cab Sim are handled using op-amps, using a charge pump to give 18v of headroom. The first output is transparent when bypassed, however, when using the second output, the Cab Sim remains engaged. This means that the Getaway Driver can be used as just a Cab Sim on its own if needed. The voicing and gain structure of this pedal is based on a cranked modded ’70s valve amp. Claim News Orange Amplification Launch Fur Coat and Getaway Driver Pedals The Fur Coat is a vintage fuzz and the Getaway Driver is an overdrive, cab sim, class A type pedal. by Guitar.com August 25, 2017 by Guitar.com August 25, 2017 When you purchase through affiliate links on Guitar.com, you may contribute to our site through commissions. Learn more Want more news stories from Guitar.com ? Follow us on Google News. The Fur Coat, inspired by the great fuzz tones from the seventies is loosely based on the old Foxx Tone Machine originally released in 1971 which was often used by artists such as Peter Frampton and Adrian Belew. Designed with a foot switchable octave, it is superbly versatile, allowing players to adjust the level of the upper octave rather than just turn it on and off. In keeping with the era’s vibe, it is built with germanium diodes and is Orange’s only true bypass pedal. When used it puts a ‘dirty, smelly fur coat’ on every note produced giving them a warm, furry quality. The Fur Coat drapes itself over the music; stroke it lovingly to produce grungy, warm effects or turn it up for lots of filthy, shaggy texture. Its tone can be dressed down casual, super modern, funky or wonderfully dramatic. ‘It sounds absolutely phenomenal’ said Clutch’s Tim Sult and Matt Pike from Sleep said “I’ve tried every fuzz pedal on the planet. This is my new favorite. The Fur Coat is everything I expected Orange would do with an octave fuzz. It’s seriously gnarly.” The action-packed Getaway Driver is an amp-in-a-box type pedal. It has the same transparent, buffered output as the Orange Two Stroke and Kongpressor pedals plus a second Cab Sim / headphone output. This makes the Getaway Driver perfect for silent practice or recording. The three dials, Volume, Bite (tone) and Gain, allow players to ‘rev their engine’. The pedal really excels when played through an amp’s clean channel, even ones with a bright cap. Low gain and high volume makes for a clean boost, pushing amps over the edge into classic overdrive. Armed with one of these, players can be transported back to the fast and furious seventies feeling the heat as this hot rod pedal drives relentlessly forward to produce the closest thing to the buzz of being a real getaway driver. ‘This pedal is great……..it sounds like vintage Orange’ observed Damon Fox The Cult/ Big Elf. The Fur Coat can be powered by 9 or 12V DC. Running at 12V increases the headroom and the output volume available. It draws very little current, less than 5mA allowing for a long battery life. The Getaway Driver can be powered by 9 or 12V DC. At 9Vs the pedal has the characteristics of EL84 valves, whereas 12Vs gives it a EL34 flavour. Posted on 2nd May 2024 1st May 2024 by Stuart First Impressions: Orange Getaway Driver Overdrive Pedal I recently bought my first Orange pedal, the Getaway Driver. The Orange Getaway Driver, on my pedalboard. What do I think of it? Read on for my First Impressions. What Did You Buy? I bought a Getaway Driver overdrive pedal, made by Orange Amplification. They’re pretty affordable, so I got mine brand new from my local guitar store . As I understand it, the Getaway Driver is an amp-in-a-box (AIAB for short) pedal that aims to capture the sound of a cranked 70’s amp. Orange doesn’t say exactly which amp, but I assume it’s going to be one that they made back in the day. Why Did You Buy It? My local guitar store has just become an Orange dealer. I don’t have a lot of experience with Orange, so I popped round to try the first shipment of gear that they had in. The Getaway Driver was one of the pedals that I tried, and in the shop it sounded different enough to be worth bringing home with me. I was drawn to two things in particular. It’s got quite a mid-rangey tone, and as I crank the gain up, the attack can get a bit rounded. Or, at least, that’s what I was hearing in the shop. Product Description The first pedal in the new Pettyjohn Electronics CORE Series, the RAIL is a true full-range fuzz machine! With this extra gain the RAIL provides significantly improved processing on the high levels at each increment of gain. Step your way from low gain distortion (which cleans up nicely) all the way up to Infinity mode. Infinity mode simulates infinite gain and is by far the craziest fuzz setting we have ever engineered, complete with a light musical gating effect. The RAIL circuit takes a unique approach to generating fuzz which does not rely on clipping diodes or finicky vintage transistors. Instead, the pedal literally boosts the signal with extreme levels of gain into the voltage rails and hence the orgin of the name "RAIL". This effect is made even more fun thanks to our dual power rail design, which can scale from +/-6v to +/-18v, with the internal supply mirroring whatever input voltage you apply via the external power supply. Completely impressed “ Double M (40W Plexi + Boosted JCM) “Hi Randy, Just want to thank you again for the fantastic work. I’m a big metal guy but seem to be playing more the Plexi side than the JCM side. Great for stuff like the Stones and AC/DC with a little punch from a tube screamer…so damm great. sources.bodyExcerpt: Recently Built Amplifiers - Phaez Amplification Skip to content Home PEDALS About Search for: Search Button Main Menu Home PEDALS About Search for: Search Button THESE ARE ALL SOLD 12W JCM type This was a custom build for a guy who has 5 Phaez amps, and this is his favourite. True JCM800 style circuit, but single EL34 in the output stage. This one has power scaling. And also a bright control. Custom order only. S.I.R. #36 Chassis only How about a chassis only version of the 25W S.I.R.#36 and 25W from a pair of EL34’s? Very cool circuit and is nice and bright. IMO there is a similarity between EVH’s amp and Slash’s. Eddie’s was BRIGHT – listen to the first chords on Runnin’ With The Devil. And listen to GNR Sweet Child O’ Mine – Slash is using his neck pickup with the tone rolled all the way off. The resulting (great) tone is into an amp that is BRIGHT! Here is a pic of one. No loop, you supply tubes. More on the SIR #36 story Custom order only. Cheyenne The Cheyenne is based on a Matchless/Vox circuit. 4XEL84 for about 35W. EF86 pentode channel and top boost treble bass channel. The Cheyenne has a loop and is a channel switcher. The Cheyenne will be supplied with a Sourmash cab, similar to the pic but you have your color choice. US$1200 (less than 1/3 of the Matchless!) Custom order only. TRIPLE F (15W EL84) Three types of Fender tones. Tweed, Twin, Bassman. 3 position rotary switch for the 3 channels. Has a loop. Fantastic. The Shadow A 5E3 type thing. 15W from a pair of 6V6’s in cathode bias. Cathodyne phase inverter as per a 5E3. One channel covers the 5E3 tones, and the other covers blackface tones. Super versatile. BLACKWATER 35W Excellent pedal platform. 2XEL34 for about 35W. DNA from Fender Blackface. FIRE AND WATER 15W 6V6 A custom build. 2 channels each with their own input. D-style ODS high gain channel and a Bassman/JTM type lower gain channel. Loop included. TAIPAN 50W 2 Channel This was a custom build and is 50W from a pair of EL34’s. H channel is based on the Framus Cobra crunch (which is based on the Soldano SLO100) and the L channel is my very well regarded and tried and true Corona channel. HIEROPHANT What is the Hierophant? It is a 100W M800+ beast. 4XEL34 in the output stage. And it does sound better than the Friedman BE100 it is sitting atop of. STARRSHA 38W KT77 This was a custom build. 2 channels – one F Blackface (Corona) and one Bassman/JTM, and it turned out fabulous. On it’s way to Australia. McClane 4XEL84 This one is the latest McClane circuit and sports 4XEL84 for about 35W. Daisycutter 6L6 Consider this one a slightly simplified version of the Atticus. Covers A WHOLE LOT OF GROUND. Loop included, and this is a channel switcher. Somewhat related to the AFD, this one has shared tonestack though, whereas the AFD has separate tonestacks for each channel. Asheville 60 Another example of the exemplary Asheville circuit and this one with 4X6L6’s that are lightly driven resulting in the tubes lasting many years. The 1-2-3 control makes it very flexible, as does the bright control. Asheville 18W The Asheville gets it DNA from the Soldano SLO100 and I have built many! This one has a pair of EL84’s for 18W. Has a loop. Loud enough for gigs, master volume works superbly so it still sounds good at low levels. I think the Asheville circuit is so refined now, it IS better than the SOLDANO – the 1.2.3 control makes it very versatile. AFD 35 A channel switcher with 2 superb M-style channels. One is crunchy/med gain and the other is med/high gain. A pair of 6L6’s in the output stage for about 35W. Loop, separate tonestacks for each channel. Would love to do another one. Blackwater 18W I was running my Savage pedal into this one and was blown away. Excellent clean amp and also a great pedal platform. Almost the same as the Rocinante just slightly different tone control HRM 35 What does HRM stand for? Hot rodded Marshall?

Sourmash head cab. There are a pair of EL34’s in the output stage and are run conservatively which leads to a long, long life. H channel is my high gain 4 stage OD Daisycutter channel, related to the Asheville but does not use a cold clipper. The L channel is my Corona (Blackface/Twin). It has a loop with a level that will not overdrive 9V pedals. Sluggo 50 Sluggo is a 50 watt EL34 amp and is somewhat related to the Atticus. A channel switcher and relays are not in the signal path when the channel is selected. Was a custom build. The H channel is my high gain 4 stage OD Daisycutter channel, related to the Asheville but does not use a cold clipper. The L channel is my Corona (Blackface/Twin). It has a loop with a level that will not overdrive 9V pedals. Continuum A custom build with a 2 Rock John Mayer as the basis. An amp more in the clean territory and has a loop. Pair of 6L6’s in the output section for about 35W. Customer was sourcing his own head cab. I don’t really like the hanging orientation as heat can build up. Variable negative feedback. Dirty Jackpot Another custom build, the Dirty Jackpot is really very impressive! Output tubes are a pair of EL84’s connected in TRIODE and results in about 7W output. This has a footswitchable boost and the core of the circuit is my AFD which is a high gain hot rodded M style circuit (it is superb!). Proper heater voltage, proper loop level. Pasadena 50W EVH’s hometown. This is one of the Pasadena’s I did with EL34’s. Has a loop. It sounds better and is more versatile than the Friedman Custom Small Box it is sitting on. I know the Friedman circuit well, not anything earth-shattering. Kodiak 4 x KT88 This thing is big and heavy lol. 4 x KT88 in output section. DNA is from an Orange AD200 Jackpot 7W A custom build and another example of triode connected EL84’s, resulting in about 7 watts. 2 channel, separate inputs. The Z input is a Z-wreck/AC30 input and the R input in my Riggs circuit which is a slightly modified Corona. There is a loop on this one too. Jomama Another custom build and related to the Atticus. A 35W channel switcher. There is a pair of EL34’s in the output stage and are run very conservatively so they should last for many years. OD high gain channel and pristine clean channel (F-based). Bluesbender The Bluesbender was a custom build and is essentially a Pasadena but with a JTM/Bassman type tonestack. 18W from a pair of EL84’s. Proper amount of feedback applied. No loop on this one. JT Special A custom build. This is a 50 watt EL34 amp and is essentially a Pasadena. This one has footswitchable boost – it is adjustable and there is an LED on when it is engaged. Yes, it has a loop too. I have the word “SUPERB” written in large letters on the schematic. Eruption Here is another custom build and the customer was sourcing the head cab. This is a single-ended amp with an EL34 in the output section and is about 11W power output. Main circuit is the Pasadena (hometown of EVH) and this amp also has a loop. Galamad 33 The Galamad was a custom build and is somewhat related to the Atticus. It has separate inputs vs channel switching. Customer was sourcing the head cab. There are a pair of 6L6’s in the output stage and are run conservatively which leads to a long long life. H channel is my high gain 4 stage OD channel, related to the Asheville but does not use a cold clipper. The L channel is my Corona (Blackface/Twin). It has a loop with a level that will not overdrive 9V pedals. Duophonic 22 This Duophonic is somewhat related to the Atticus but it has separate inputs vs channel
